canberra.title: Stepfather’s alleged assault leaves 10-year-old with significant bruises
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged family violence. The alleged assault a stepfather inflicted on his 10-year-old stepson we...
canberra.content:
12 August 2026

A 29-year-old man sobbed in the ACT Magistrates Court when he was charged with assaulting a child. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged family violence.

The alleged assault a stepfather inflicted on his 10-year-old stepson went undetected until the boy spoke to others at his school, a court has heard.

The 29-year-old man faced the ACT Magistrates Court on Wednesday (12 August) on a charge of assault and was seen sobbing while he was guarded by three corrections officers who appeared to be wearing body armour, gloves and helmets.

The court heard he was alleged to have assaulted the boy. Pictures showed significant bruising to the child’s arm.

The boy originally said the bruising was caused while playing sport at school, but the court heard he had been suspended when the injuries were noticed.

He later told people at the school that his stepfather caused the injuries.

Prosecutor Isabel Michael told the court the boy reported he didn’t feel safe during the alleged incident and felt safer once his mother arrived.

But the court also heard the mother denied the alleged assault occurred and Magistrate Heidi Robinson said she was worried the woman was not acting protectively towards her son.

Ms Michael opposed bail, saying the boy had a sibling and there were safety concerns for both children.

But the man’s lawyer, Pia Beohm of Legal Aid, said he had been sober since he was last released from custody and the progress he made in the community to move away from drugs and alcohol would be affected if he was returned to jail.

She also said the period during which the 10-year-old boy was questioned about a bruise was of concern.

Magistrate Robinson said she had some concerns about the man interfering with witnesses. But she was satisfied the risks of his release could be mitigated with bail conditions.

The man, who is not named to protect the boy’s identity, was granted bail on conditions including that he not contact the boy, the sibling or the mother.

The matter was adjourned to September. No plea was entered.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 02 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 02 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call triple zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to police by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

canberra.title: Former ADF member allegedly involved in major weapons manufacturing operation
canberra.snippet: Police suspect a former member of the Australian Defence Force (ADF) who was allegedly caught with an illegal stash of firearms may have ...
canberra.content:
12 August 2026

Pepper spray, knuckle dusters and a firearm were allegedly seized from a 35-year-old man’s home in Taylor. Photos: ACT Policing.

Police suspect a former member of the Australian Defence Force (ADF) who was allegedly caught with an illegal stash of firearms may have been involved in a major weapons-making operation in Canberra.

Officers raided the 35-year-old man’s home in Taylor last week where they allegedly discovered 3D-printed handguns and handgun parts as well as about 30 3D-printed knuckle dusters, 12 tasers and seven cans of pepper spray.

“During the search, officers located weapons packaged in shipping bags, which police allege indicates the items were being prepared for sale and distribution,” an ACT Policing spokesperson said.

“The items were seized by police along with a 3D printer and computer which will undergo forensic examination.”

The man was arrested on Friday (7 August) and applied for bail in the ACT Magistrates Court on Wednesday (12 August), where a police officer told the court the investigation had only begun the day before his arrest.

“We believe that there is a larger scale manufacturing operation going on,” the officer said.

The officer alleged that police found hundreds of postage bags and stamps at the man’s home, suggesting he was selling items.

He said while the alleged weapons had been seized from the home, both 3D printers and the software used to operate them were easy to obtain.

The court also heard the man was believed to have operated an online locksmith-related business. Under questioning by the man’s lawyer, Mitchell Greig of Hugo Law Group, the officer admitted it was understandable that someone might have a lot of packaging if they ran an online business like that.

Pepper spray, knuckle dusters and a firearm were allegedly seized from a 35-year-old man’s home in Taylor. Photos: ACT Policing.

Prosecutor Isabel Michael opposed bail, saying the man was alleged to have made and possessed “very dangerous” weapons.

She said the allegations demonstrated he appeared to have a professional and sophisticated knowledge of weapon and firearm manufacturing.

Ms Michael also said police were concerned he might restart his alleged 3D printing operations and he could access and delete online accounts linked to the investigation if granted bail.

Mr Grieg said his client had no prior criminal history and had strong and tangible reasons to remain in the ACT, including supporting his family.

“The consequences of continuing remand are profound for [the man],” he said.

Mr Greig said police had already accessed his client’s mobile phone and that it would be unreasonable to refuse bail on the basis that investigators had yet to access online material in the matter.

But the court also heard there were mental health concerns for the man and there was a long discussion about how to best support these.

Magistrate Heidi Robinson ultimately said she would adjourn the matter for a mental health assessment and then determine the bail application on 21 August.

Region will not name the man while the assessment takes place.

The former ADF member has entered pleas of not guilty to one count of the unauthorised manufacture of a firearm and four counts of possessing a prohibited weapon without authorisation.

canberra.title: CIT Board chair open to closer UC ties but merger a government decision
canberra.snippet: Canberra Institute of Technology Board chair Tom Rogers says any merger with the University of Canberra was a matter for the ACT Governme...
canberra.content:
CIT Board chair Tom Rogers is optimistic but says finances can’t stay in the red. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

Canberra Institute of Technology Board chair Tom Rogers says any merger with the University of Canberra was a matter for the ACT Government, but he is open to any arrangement that will help put the cash-strapped training organisation on a more sustainable path.

Mr Rogers was speaking with an eye firmly on the future, after CIT cut loose its embattled CEO Dr Margot McNeill.

He said CIT had to take a serious look at its finances.

“I would like to see us with the best possible structure to support our students, and if that means we work more closely with other education providers, I’m absolutely open to that, and I know the board would be as well,” Mr Rogers said.

UC Vice-Chancellor Bill Shorten is understood to back a merger that retained CIT’s identity and brand.

The university and CIT signed a deal last year that opened degree pathways for CIT students, and Mr Shorten has been vocal about greater facility sharing.

But the board had no authority to approve a merger and government would need to be involved in any formal arrangement.

The ACT Government is reviewing CIT’s governance arrangements and, as a stakeholder, UC is being consulted.

This afternoon (12 August), Skills, Training and Industrial Relations Minister Michael Pettersson issued a statement welcoming Dr McNeill’s resignation.

“I welcome the news this matter has come to a close, and we can now move forward,” he said.

“The ACT Government will continue to progress the review into CIT’s governance to ensure the appropriate settings are in place.”

Mr Rogers said CIT was also open to more connections with UNSW Canberra and TAFE NSW.

“If we can do some stuff that makes sense, with other organisations, and it does save money for the taxpayer, it’s something we’d look at clearly,” he said.

He said the ACT Government hadn’t spoken to him about a merger, “but I’m going to keep talking to Bill because obviously they’re a very close partner of ours and we want to make sure that we’re doing as much as we can”.

“If there’s genuine financial benefits and efficiencies of scale, it would be a bit wrong for me to say to the ACT taxpayer, well, we’re not doing that,” Mr Rogers said.

“These are things that you’ll absolutely look at. That’s why I’m meeting with Bill in a couple of weeks to make sure that our linkages are as strong as they can be within the current framework, and let’s see what happens.”

CIT could find savings in a merger with UC. Photo: UC.

Mr Rogers said CIT could not keep running up deficits like last year’s $28 million result and go cap in hand to government for top-ups.

It was now looking to shave 10 per cent off its annual operating budget, including through voluntary redundancies.

Mr Rogers stressed this did not mean cutting staff by 10 per cent or courses, although the offering would and should be continually updated.

“We’ve got to look at all areas of our operation, and in any public sector organisation, there’s stuff that can be done differently,” he said.

But none of that should detract from student learning.

Mr Rogers rejected criticisms that CIT was top-heavy with executives at the expense of teaching staff, saying that may have been the case in the past, but the board was now “right-sizing” the organisation.

It had taken steps to ensure CIT was governed effectively, and a recently advertised $172,000 position was not an executive role but a much-needed specialist procurement position in an area that had drawn fire from critics.

He said it was undeniable that CIT’s reputation had been damaged, not just in past months but in the years since the Leanne Cover contracts scandal, but it was the board’s job now to rebuild that reputation and win the trust of staff.

He welcomed scrutiny as long as it didn’t degenerate into criticising everything CIT did.

Mr Rogers remained optimistic about CIT’s and the sector’s future.

“TAFE’s time has come. We need to seize that at the same time, and I think our brand will be important to that,” he said.

canberra.title: The labyrinthic world of Elisa Crossing’s paintings
canberra.snippet: Elisa Crossing has been exhibiting in Canberra since 1986. She has been associated with the Canberra School of Art, in its various manife...
canberra.content:
12 August 2026

Start the conversation

Elisa Crossing, Intermission, 2026, oil on linen. Photo: Civic Art Bureau.

Elisa Crossing has been exhibiting in Canberra since 1986. She has been associated with the Canberra School of Art, in its various manifestations, for much of her professional life, initially as a student and subsequently as a lecturer.

Over the years she has developed a peculiar artistic language in which there is a tension between a cerebral conceptual framework and the quite sensuous resolution of the work.

Her exhibition at the Civic Art Bureau consists of 19 ‘clever paintings’ that combine closely observed realistic detail with an ambiguous frame of reference, at times laced with a bit of dry wit.

One could say that virtually everything that one sees in her paintings does exist in the observable world or in other paintings, but not in the same configurations as one discovers in her works.

She loves conceptual games of placing paintings within paintings, playing with fragments of deserted airports, merging interior and exterior spaces, and using reflections and patterns.

She appears to enjoy stopping the viewer in their tracks, inviting them to enter and explore the painting, and to discover or invent their own reality within it.

There is frequently a semantic game involved in the titles of her paintings and exhibitions, one called the self-explanatory Slow looking and the present exhibition titled ‘Move me!’

The artist explains that the title is drawn from the question a viewer may pose to the artist: what does the painter want from her audience? She wants the viewer to be moved by the paintings.

Elisa Crossing, 5 o’clock shadow, 2026, oil on linen, 61 x 92cm, Photo: Civic Art Bureau.

“Move me! is an exploration of the active and embodied nature of looking. It builds on the theme of Slow looking, which has been central to my practice for many years and is a position that runs counter to the ethos of the digital economy, which venerates speed and promises us the joy of ‘frictionless’ experiences,” Crossing explains,

“For me, friction is essential to the process of painting and how we make meaning from it.”

If we engage with one of her smaller canvases, 5 o’clock shadow, it is built on a series of objects found within an interior space and caught within a web of shadows.

The colloquial meaning of 5 o’clock shadow is the short stubble that appears on a bloke’s face by late afternoon following the morning shave.

In the painting, there is an encrustation of afternoon shadows within an interior space that, at least for this viewer, hints at a possible feeling for the uncanny, something that is familiar and yet possesses a touch of the eerie.

Elisa Crossing, Press play, 2026, oil on linen, 122 x 105cm, Photo: Civic Art Bureau.

The painting Intermission is one of the more ambitious works at the exhibition. It combines a fragment from Jean-Honoré Fragonard’s Rococo classic painting The Swing, c1767, with various interior spaces. As with many artists, Fragonard’s painting casts a haunting and enigmatic presence, and Crossing suggests many different ways of seeing and feeling it.

Her layering of lush realities with the spartan realities of the studio builds a surface tension that is both seductive and intriguing.

The large studio interior space in Press play is perhaps less intriguing and more accessible until we notice the frame-within-a-frame reference, suggesting a mixture of different realities.

The framing of different realities and the idea of a painting within a painting, most beautifully presented in her Vanishing day, are common strategies throughout this exhibition.

Crossing appears to enjoy teasing and intriguing her viewers with enigmatic spaces that, at first glance, may seem like visual puzzles but are not, in that they have no real solutions.

Crossing presents a series of visual entrapments that will seduce the viewer who pauses long enough in front of them to create their own narratives about these beautifully realised and carefully observed oil paintings.

Elisa Crossing, Vanishing day, 2026, oil on linen, 61 x 92cm, Photo: Civic Art Bureau

Elisa Crossing, Move me!, is at Civic Art Bureau, Melbourne Building, upstairs at Smiths Alternative, 76 Alinga St, Civic. It closes on 31 August. Open Thursday to Saturday, from 12 pm to 5 pm, and Sunday, from 2 pm to 5 pm.

canberra.title: Follow the smell of sourdough to this hidden Braddon pizza truck
canberra.snippet: The buzz is building for one of Braddon’s newest food trucks, Bella Pizza. Tucked down what is essentially a driveway at the rear of Wave...
canberra.content:
It’s a little hidden, but the discovery of some delicious pizza is worth it. Photo: Martin Conway.

The buzz is building for one of Braddon’s newest food trucks, Bella Pizza. Tucked down what is essentially a driveway at the rear of Waves Carwash and opening right on the start of winter, it hasn’t been the easiest start for owners Sanjay and Radhika, but they’re determined to have all of Canberra enjoying their 24-hour fermented sourdough bases.

It’s an unlikely location to find good food, and that’s what I love about it; it offers a sense of discovery rarely found in a polished restaurant or fancy fit-out, propped up there between a roller door and the passing cars looking for a spot.

It’s businesses like these that will help Braddon not tip too far over into the tight grip of gentrification.

“We were initially thinking about opening a cafe or a takeaway, but the costs are so high, and we’re always inspired by the food trucks in Canberra and Sydney, so we thought we would give that a go,” explains owner Sanjay Ghatani, who has started the business with his wife Radhika Dhungana.

The smiling face of Radhika Dhungana greets customers at Bella Pizza. Photo: Tenele Conway.

Starting a food truck may have been the more affordable option, but finding a place to park it proved more challenging, and Sanjay and Radhika sat on the truck for more than 6 months before securing a spot at the carwash.

Settled into their new home, Sanjay is now bringing together more than a decade of experience in pizza kitchens across Canberra to deliver a food-truck experience he hopes will really hit the spot with Canberrans.

“The secret really is the fermented sourdough base; people love that it’s very light, and we focus on quality ingredients like fior di latte cheese. It costs more, but it’s worth it,” Sanjay explains.

The menu consists of seven varieties of pizza, plus two additional kids’ pizzas and a selection of starters like mixed olives, confit garlic cheese pizza, pizza bianca and some surprise momos (because who doesn’t love a momo?)

“The menu I created are pizzas that are most popular in a fine dining restaurant, plus a few I created myself. The pork and potato pizza is our most popular. The pork is Italian sausage, and the potato is marinated with Italian herbs and rosemary and pre-cooked to get a really good rich flavour from them.”

The Ham and Pine pizza is not to be confused with the Hawaiian Pizza on the kids menu. Photo: Martin Conway.

Choosing what pizzas to have is always the test of a relationship, and I’m afflicted with a husband who always insists on ordering a ham and pineapple pizza, so on our recent visit I compromised and allowed it; that’s just the kind of wife I am, and we paired it with the Tre Carne Meatlovers.

There was actually nothing to stress about with Sanjay’s Ham and Pine pizza, since it isn’t your standard Hawaiian pizza (they’ve saved that for the kids).

This version has the lovely San Marzano tomato base that appears across the full range, fior di latte cheese, double-smoked leg ham, and Sanjay’s special cinnamon-fusion pineapple. It has none of that cheap, sharp tinned-fruit flavour that I was expecting; in fact, the pineapple just added a subtle sweetness and balanced well with all the flavours on the base.

The Tre Carne is a wonderful blending of quality meats on their signature San Marzano sauce. Photo: Martin Conway.

The Tre Carne is a wonderful blend of rich, high-quality Italian meats, including Italian sausage, double-smoked leg ham, and pepperoni. Sitting on top of that same smooth tomato base, it’s a harmonious combination that’s a real winner.

Looking forward to the warmer months and longer afternoons at his Braddon location, Sanjay says the next dream for the business would be to head to Italy to build on his already extensive pizza experience.

Bella Pizza is located at the rear of 17 Lonsdale Street, Braddon, and is open from Tuesday until Sunday from 5 pm.

australia.title: Barnaby Joyce claims One Nation ‘one of the gayest parties in Australia’ as former candidate’s comments surface
australia.snippet: One Nation MP says failed WA candidate’s comments describing same-sex attraction as a mental illness are ‘highly offensive’ Get our break...
australia.content:
Barnaby Joyce has defended One Nation as “one of the gayest parties in Australia” after comments surfaced from one of its failed candidates describing same-sex attraction as a mental illness.

The former National turned One Nation MP was asked to respond to a series of homophobic comments made by a former Western Australian legislative council candidate for One Nation in a video last month, as first reported by ABC on Wednesday afternoon.

Parminder Singh, who was third on the party’s ticket at the WA election in 2025, told online personality Jasky Singh, known as Mr Sikkant, that he believed gay people have a mental illness and that marriage equality should not have been legalised.

Though Singh claimed not to have a problem with gay people, he took issue with them “advertising” their sexuality.

“You [don’t] need to gay parade in city,” he said.

Guardian Australia has contacted Singh for comment.

Joyce was asked about Singh’s comments on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing after a page linking to his candidacy was taken down from One Nation’s website.

The One Nation MP said while he didn’t have the power to disendorse someone, the comments were “highly offensive”.

“He obviously doesn’t know One Nation because we got a surprise for him. We have quite a large proportion of gay people,” he said.

“We believe in an Australian culture that is tolerant, egalitarian, and has things that are inside the guardrails and outside … this is outside the guardrails.”

Joyce added that he believed his political party was “one of the gayest parties in Australia”.

One Nation’s South Australian MP James Virgo is gay.

Anna Brown, the chief executive of Equality Australia, described Singh’s comments as “demonstrably false, thoroughly discredited and deeply harmful”.

“People can hear what these candidates have to say and make their own judgment about whether those views reflect the Australia they want to live in, and whether they are consistent with contemporary Australian values,” Brown said.

“Almost two-thirds of the nearly 80% of Australians who took part in the 2017 postal survey voted in support of marriage equality.

“That overwhelming result tells us far more about the values of modern Australia than the outdated and offensive views of this individual.”

Singh’s comments come as One Nation readies its candidates ahead of the Victorian state election in November.

The minor party’s vetting process has been criticised for lacking thorough examination.

Most recently, One Nation was forced to dump one of its candidates, Aoi Baxter, ahead of the South Australian state election after the ABC revealed a warrant for his arrest had been issued in the UK for allegedly sexually touching a woman in 2024 without consent.

Joyce said the minor party’s candidate selection process would improve as the party grew.

“When something’s growing like that, you’re going to have growing pains … and your internal resources won’t be able to keep up with the membership as it goes, and the applicants as they go,” he said.

“As we grow and we get the resources, and we also become more proficient. People are allowed to have views, of course – but they’ve got to be within the Australian guardrails. That’s one of our key policies.”

australia.title: ‘Send food photos’: Lobbyist paid for former premier’s brother to go to Fiji to avoid inquiry, Icac hears
australia.snippet: Lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood gives evidence about allegations linked to Reformers at Independent Commission Against Corruption hearing Get o...
australia.content:
A Liberal figure under investigation for allegedly accepting illegal political donations has told an inquiry he paid for the brother of former premier Dominic Perrottet to travel to Fiji and urged the CEO of Catholic Schools NSW to “go to Brisbane” to avoid appearing before a parliamentary committee.

Consultant and lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood gave his third day of evidence to the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s (Icac) Operation Rosny on Wednesday.

Icac is investigating whether the Christian Liberal group the Reformers solicited or accepted prohibited donations for the recruitment or renewal of members to the party. The practice, known as branch stacking, is not itself illegal.

The Reformers wanted more conservative policies on issues such as same-sex marriage, abortion and euthanasia. Greenwood has disputed that he was a member of the group.

Questioning on Wednesday afternoon focused on a New South Wales parliamentary inquiry into allegations of branch stacking which preceded Icac’s probe.

Icac has previously heard that Greenwood, Reformers Christian Ellis and Jean-Claude Perrottet, as well as Charles Perrottet, another brother of the former premier, avoided summons to appear at public hearings in 2023. Dominic Perrottet is not named as a person of interest in Icac’s allegations.

Greenwood on Wednesday admitted to giving Jean-Claude Perrottet his credit card details so he could book flights to Fiji. The inquiry heard that he also arranged for three loans worth $25,000 to be paid to him for the trip in February 2023 via his lobbying firm JPG Advisory.

The inquiry heard that after another person named in Icac’s allegations, Catholic Schools CEO, Dallas McInerney, received a letter from the chair of the parliamentary inquiry, Greenwood sent him a message in which he said: “WTF. Go to Brisbane”. Greenwood said he did not recall sending the messages.

Greenwood admitted that he himself had avoided summons he considered “invalid”, accepting the offer of a private security guard outside his home from Sharangan Maheswaran, who is also named in Icac’s allegations, and was a lawyer to fugitive property developer Jean Nassif and his company Toplace.

Icac is investigating the allegation that, between 2020 and 2023, Nassif made prohibited donations to Greenwood, Ellis and Charles Perrottet in exchange for outcomes sought by Nassif.

The inquiry heard messages between Greenwood and a private investigator employed by Maheswaran about security guards in which he requested “no numpties. Attentive ones”.

Greenwood, who said that it was his idea for Jean-Claude Perrottet to go to Fiji, admitted he suggested to Maheswaran that Nassif cover his costs.

“I can’t remember if it was paid, but I suggested to Sharangan at the time: ‘You know, your boss is the cause of this, so you can cover it.’”

The inquiry heard Greenwood wrote to Jean-Claude Perrottet “to send food photos” from Fiji, and that the latter negotiated a $165,000 employment contract with Catholic Schools NSW while he avoided the parliamentary inquiry in 2023.

The inquiry previously heard from Reformer Robert Assaf that he had met with Greenwood on multiple occasions this year after receiving summons to appear before Icac, leaving their phones in the car.

On Wednesday, the inquiry heard that Greenwood also met with Jean-Claude Perrottet at a pub in Sydney after Greenwood’s compulsory examinations with the watchdog in June 2025, during which the Icac commissioner instructed him not to discuss his evidence with anyone except his lawyers.

Greenwood was asked why in the meeting, of which the watchdog has CCTV, the men positioned their phones away from the table. He said it was “a practice I’ve had for a long time”.

“I remember Barack Obama once said he never brings a phone into a meeting,” he said.

Greenwood said he had spoken to Ellis, who has moved to the UK and is not expected to give evidence, twice this week in phone calls after hearings. After he said Ellis had watched the end of the livestream on Tuesday’s proceedings, counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC addressed Ellis directly.

“Commissioner, can I just take the opportunity to reiterate, if Mr Ellis is listening, that we have contacted Mr Ellis and requested that he give evidence in this commission, and offered to make arrangements so that he can give evidence to this commission via video proceedings from the United Kingdom, and that those arrangements can be made.”

The presiding commissioner, Fabian Gleeson, said: “Yes, you may. And if Mr Ellis is listening, the commission waits for his response.”

Earlier on Wednesday, the inquiry heard Reformers members received a “kickback” from consultancy payments made by Catholic Schools NSW, the governing body for more than 600 schools in the state.

The inquiry has heard that Greenwood agreed to pay Jean-Claude Perrottet, whom he described as his “best mate”, half of a monthly retainer if he was able to secure the contract with McInerney, while Assaf received a one-off 10% of the retainer.

Greenwood was read emails between him and McInerney in October 2022 in which the latter asked him about missing invoices, to which he responded: “I stopped sending them in the end, haha.”

Dwyer, asking why he had signed off the message in that way, said: “Is the joke on parents paying funds to Catholic Schools NSW, or the government assisting with that funding, that this money is not for any genuine consultancy, but was in fact intended in part to fund Jean-Claude Perrottet?”

“Absolutely not,” said Greenwood.

Nearly 80% of funding for Catholic Schools NSW comes from federal and state funding, or about $3.8bn in 2024.

Wednesday’s evidence involved several fiery exchanges. At one point, Greenwood was reprimanded during his evidence after he told someone in the hearing room: “Don’t give me that look.”

The presiding commissioner, Fabian Gleeson, pausing the hearing, told Greenwood: “You need to be respectful in the way in which you behave. You need to listen to counsel’s questions. You do not direct comments to other people sitting in this room.”

As Greenwood was cross examined by Bruce Levet, the lawyer representing former NSW Liberal minister David Elliott, about a “shit sheet” Greenwood has admitted commissioning on Elliott, he accused the former MP of “stalking my mother right now … on LinkedIn”.

Gleeson said: “You definitely should not have said that, Mr Greenwood … It was totally inappropriate.” Greenwood apologised.

Greenwood has not been released from his summons and is expected to appear again before the commission. McInerney is due to appear as a witness on Thursday and Friday this week.

Icac’s inquiry continues.

    Welcome

What we learned today, Wednesday 12 August

That’s where we’ll leave our live news coverage for the day.

Before we go, let’s recap the day’s top headlines:

  • The One Nation deputy leader, Barnaby Joyce, has called his party “one of the gayest in Australia”.

  • The shadow housing minister, Andrew Bragg, has stood by his proposal to lower net migration to 180,000 a year in a wide-ranging speech in which he lamented not stopping the Morrison government’s “madness” – even as colleagues side-stepped supporting the target figure publicly.

  • The Commonwealth Bank has reported a bumper $10.9bn full-year cash profit, up 7%, in its full-year financial results.

  • The Victorian parliament has voted to abolish group voting tickets (GVTs) to elect its upper house.

  • Australia has joined the US and dozens of other nations, including the UK, France, Germany and the Philippines, in calling on all relevant countries to provide advanced notice of ballistic missile launches.

  • Melon-gate continues, with the Coalition demanding an AFP investigation while the Japanese ambassador downplayed the prime minister’s comments on a comedy podcast.

  • Victoria will begin vaccinating about 5,000 little penguins at Phillip Island and St Kilda from next week to protect them against the deadly H5 bird flu, in what is believed to be the world’s largest vaccination program involving wild birds.

  • The teals have brought some of the best merch we’ve seen in parliament, as they try to pressure the government and opposition to go harder on gambling advertising.

  • The prosecution’s case against Naveed Akram for his alleged role as a gunman in the Bondi terror attack now includes 12 additional electronic devices and a report on an explosive device.

Thanks for sticking around, we’ll see you tomorrow!

SafeWork SA investigates death of 26-year-old man at Adelaide Hills worksite

SafeWork South Australia says it is investigating the death of a 26-year-old man at a worksite at Charleston in the Adelaide Hills.

Police say the man’s body was found at the worksite this morning.

The workplace safety regulator says its inspectors attended the site and are continuing to investigate what led to the man’s death.

Petra Stock

EPBC assessment of giant cuttlefish sought after ‘unprecedented decline’

The Great Southern Reef Foundation – together with leading cephalopod scientists Prof Bronwyn Gillanders and Associate Prof Zoe Doubleday – has written to the environment minister, Murray Watt, requesting he urgently consider a unique population of giant Australian cuttlefish for protection under national environment laws, after an “unprecedented decline”.

The population of giant Australian cuttlefish in South Australia’s Upper Spencer Gulf “forms the only known mass breeding aggregation of any cuttlefish species anywhere on earth”, the letter said.

This year, the animals largely failed to arrive at their established breeding grounds near Whyalla. An independent July survey recorded only 44 adults and about 440 eggs over 8 hours underwater across the breeding coast, pointing to an unprecedented decline.

While these observations are not directly comparable with the government’s population estimates, the official estimate was 63,374 cuttlefish in 2025 and 81,420 in 2024. The long-term average from 1998 to 2019 was approximately 110,000.

The marine scientists have requested “the shortest practicable assessment timeframe” and support for “immediate research and contingency planning while the assessment proceeds”.

Read more about the cuttlefish here:

Clare O’Neil condemns Andrew Bragg’s 'crazed' National Press Club speech

The federal housing minister, Clare O’Neil, has criticised shadow housing minister Andrew Bragg’s National Press Club address, saying the speech was “unhinged”.

The speech from Andrew Bragg today was a crazed, almost manic ideological fever dream that ranged from repeated references to communism and the Morrison government’s madness to calling superannuation state-sponsored corruption. It was genuinely unhinged.

A key point of Bragg’s speech suggested reducing the National Construction Code from more than 2,000 pages to 80. O’Neil said she agreed that the housing construction code was “too complex” but added that rewriting it would require a “diligent reform process” involving the sector.

The idea that we will go to an 80-page construction code, what Andrew Bragg is saying, to be clear to Australians, is that we should scrap housing standards.

There is no one serious in this debate who is saying the answer to our housing problems is to scrap housing standards. At the end of the day, Australian consumers pay for that. If we create homes that don’t have heating and cooling, Australians have to pay for that through higher energy prices.

‘We are one of the gayest parties in Australia’: Barnaby Joyce condemns candidate’s homophobic comments

The One Nation deputy leader, Barnaby Joyce, has criticised a series of homophobic statements made by the party’s WA candidate, Parminder Singh, including the claim that homosexuality is a “mental illness”.

Singh, who was on One Nation WA’s upper house ticket at the 2025 election, made the comments during an interview posted to social media by Perth comedian and content creator Jasky Singh.

Speaking to ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Joyce called the comments offensive, adding that One Nation is “one of the gayest parties in Australia”.

He obviously doesn’t know One Nation because we have, surprisingly, quite a large proportion of gay people. They are all the same: they don’t want to be glorified or vilified; they just want people to accept them. They go on and do a very good job and, to be quite frank, a comment like that is highly offensive in my view.

One Nation’s South Australian MP James Virgo is gay.

Joyce has not confirmed whether Singh will be disendorsed.

Ask Guardian’s political team a question

Do you have a question you’d like to ask Guardian Australia’s team of political reporters in Canberra this week?

The Australian Politics podcast is recording an “Ask me anything” episode with Tom McIlroy, Krishani Dhanji, Josh Butler and Sarah Basford-Canales. We’d love readers to send through questions for us, so please email us at australianpolitics@theguardian.com.

Looking forward to hearing from you!

Benita Kolovos

Lidia Thorpe on Victorian government bill that scraps open air rights

Senator Lidia Thorpe has accused the Victorian Labor government of using its historic treaty with First Nations people as a “photo opportunity”, as it pushes ahead with a controversial bill that would scrap the requirement to give prisoners at least one hour of open air daily.

Gellung Warl, Victoria’s First Peoples’ representative body, has for the first time exercised its powers under the Statewide Treaty Act to call on the government to withdraw the corrections amendment bill 2026, which is expected to pass this week.

The bill would give authorities the ability to deny prisoners their daily hour of outdoor time “subject to operational considerations” – a move the Victorian government itself has acknowledged is incompatible with the state’s Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities and partly incompatible with its treaty with First Nations People.

In a statement to Guardian Australia, Thorpe said the new premier, Ben Carroll, should show he’s committed to a real partnership with First Peoples by withdrawing the bill. She said:

Labor celebrated Treaty, took their selfies and filled their socials with how historic it was. But Treaty means nothing if the Government ignores First Peoples when they exercise the powers that Treaty gives them.

We saw the same bad faith when they signed Treaty and announced their cruel “adult crime, adult time” laws in the same week, despite knowing the disproportionate harm this would cause to our children. They also admitted those laws are incompatible with the Victorian Human Rights Charter.

For this Labor government, Treaty is a photo opportunity. For our people, it is about peace, justice and a genuine change in the relationship.

Premier Allan took a bad faith approach to Treaty. The new Premier has an opportunity to reset that and show that he is committed to real partnership with First Peoples. That should mean withdrawing this bill and stopping the harm it will cause to our people, at least until he has worked through it with Gellung Warl in good faith.

More here:

Penry Buckley

Icac hears evidence Liberal upper house MP helped Reformers wanting to avoid inquiry

The NSW Icac has heard evidence that NSW upper house Liberal frontbencher Chris Rath helped members of the Reformers who wanted to avoid summons to appear before a parliamentary inquiry in 2023 that preceded Icac’s probe.

Jeremy Greenwood has been read a message he sent to Jean-Claude Perrottet, in which he wrote: “We need to know when the summons is being issued. Can Chris find out?” He says he assumes this refers to Rath and admits he was asking Jean-Claude Perrottet to find out details from a sitting member of parliament to avoid service of summons.

He says Rath later sent him a photo a committee paper with his old address that said process servers had attempted to service him a summons there. He is read a message from Jean-Claude Perrottet advising of a committee meeting on serving summons. “Rath will tell us result after,” Jean-Claude Perrottet wrote.

The opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, has declined to make a decision about Rath’s future on her frontbench until after Icac’s hearings conclude. Rath has been referred to the parliamentary privileges committee over the incident.

In a statement after a Sydney Morning Herald report about the assistance he had provided to members of the Reformers, Rath, who later recused himself from the inquiry committee, said he was “apologetic” for the incident: He said:

This inquiry commenced in the highly politically charged context of an election campaign, and at the time I didn’t comprehend the gravity of the allegations … I am not under investigation by Icac, nor have I been called as a witness to the inquiry or asked to provide any evidence.

Petra Stock

Melbourne Royal Show poultry competition cancelled due to H5 bird flu

Organisers for the Melbourne Royal Show have cancelled the poultry competition this year, as a precautionary step given uncertainty about the spread of H5 bird flu.

The show’s executive general manager, Hannah von Bibra, said:

Following consultation with Agriculture Victoria and the Chief Veterinary Officer team, Melbourne Royal is taking this precautionary step to protect the health and wellbeing of the Victorian poultry community.

Whilst there are currently no detections of H5N1 in Australian poultry, the situation is not predictable and, as such, we want to give our community as much certainty as possible.

The Melbourne Royal Show is planned for 24 September to 4 October.

The decision followed an announcement last week that the Royal Adelaide Show, scheduled for September, would cancel all of its bird shows and exhibits.

Icac hears witness used security guard to evade 'invalid' parliamentary summons and paid for Reformer’s Fiji trip

Penry Buckley

Returning to the Icac’s Operation Rosny, questions have returned to a NSW parliamentary inquiry into allegations of branch stacking that preceded Icac’s probe.

Witness Jeremy Greenwood has admitted he evaded a summons to appear before the inquiry in 2023, saying he believed the summons was “invalid”. He says he used a private security guard who was stationed outside his home for two or three days, after speaking to Sharangan Maheswaran, also named in Icac’s allegations, then a lawyer to fugitive property developer Jean Nassif.

Icac is investigating the allegation whether between 2020 and 2023 Nassif made prohibited donations to Liberal figures including Greenwood in exchange for outcomes he had sought for developer Toplace. Greenwood, who initially said he had requested Toplace pay for the security guard, said that Maheswaran had offered the security guard’s services.

Greenwood has also admitted to paying for Reformer Jean-Claude Perrottet to travel to Fiji during the inquiry to avoid appearing, giving him his credit card details to pay for his flight. He also provided him with three separate loans totalling $25,000 invoiced through his lobbying firm JPG Advisory. He says he suggested to Maheswaran “You know your boss is the cause of this, so you can cover it”.

Counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, asks:

By your boss, you meant Jean Nassif could pick up the tab for what you were paying for the premier’s brother, John Claude Perrottet, to stay in Fiji to avoid summons to appear at a parliamentary inquiry?

Greenwood accepts this, saying Jean-Claude Perrottet had not yet paid for the cost of the trip. He says he cannot recall if the cost of the trip was passed on to Toplace “but I suggested [it] to Sharangan at the time”.

Krishani Dhanji

Thanks for following along on the blog today! I’ll leave you with Achol Arok and see you here bright and early tomorrow.

Tl;dr here’s what happened in question time

  • The Coalition gave us a mixed bag of questions today, including three on melon-gate, and others on health insurance premiums and tax reforms, but it was again a somewhat lowkey affair – no big drama and no cutting zingers.

  • The prime minister repeatedly refused to apologise over melon-gate and batted off questions over whether his office or department leaked a memo on the issue from the Japanese government.

  • The health minister, Mark Butler, accused the opposition of parroting modelling by the insurance lobby over a question on how many Australians would be affected by Labor cutting premium rebates for over 65s.

  • Milton Dick made a few of us laugh by saying he owns up to his mistakes, after giving the crossbench a question prematurely.

  • And Anthony Albanese said there’s been no influence over the Labor’s gambling policy by the industry, after independent Andrew Wilkie wrote to the anti-corruption watchdog claiming the government “improperly influenced” by wagering lobby.

Japanese embassy downplays Albanese melon comments

Josh Butler

Japan’s ambassador to Australia has downplayed Anthony Albanese’s comments about melons and Sanae Takaichi, saying the Australian government had reassured them that the prime minister “did not make the comments in the way that has been reported”.

While the Coalition is continuing to raise outrage over Albanese’s comments to the Bush Deep podcast, the Japanese government appears to be uninterested in making a diplomatic incident out of the ill-timed comments.

“We are aware of the reporting in the media. We have been informed by the Australian side that Prime Minister Albanese did not make the comments in the way that has been reported,” said a statement from the Japanese ambassador, Kazuhiro Suzuki.

The statement went on to say that Albanese’s hosting of Takaichi in Australia in May was “held in a very relaxed atmosphere, and we believe it helped build a personal trust relationship between the two leaders”.

The melon comments have been canvassed regularly by some media outlets since the podcast first aired in July. But it resurfaced as a political issue after The Australian ran a comment piece on Monday from the former Japanese ambassador Shingo Yamagami, who left his post in 2023, who claimed Albanese had insulted Takaichi.

And with a final dixer to skills minister Andrew Giles, the PM calls time on QT for another day – just one to go.

Third time unlucky, Coalition try again on melon-gate

Ted O’Brien has tried once again, and failed, to corner the prime minister and call on him to apologise over melon-gate.

He asks if Albanese will “follow the example of someone else in this House, who has made it very clear, when he made a mistake, he owns up to it” (see below!)

Anthony Albanese once again doesn’t want a bar of it and instead spruiks the relationship between Australia and Japan, saying the two countries have “never been more strategically aligned than we are today”.

‘When I make mistakes I own up to them’: Milton Dick

Milton Dick has brought (half) the House down after prematurely giving Sophie Scamps the call, and then offering a cheeky joke in admitting his mistake.

Angus Taylor gives him a big nod and a chuckle as Dick says, “I will admit I made the mistake there. And, when I make mistakes I own up to them.”

It gets a big laugh from the Coalition benches.

But because Scamps has already asked her question – about whether the government will implement a sugar tax – Mark Butler answers it.

Butler says the short answer is that there are “no plans” to tax sugary products like they have in the UK.

There’s different views about a tax in the community, there’s overwhelming support for better front of packet labelling. We introduced that scheme back when I was the assistant minister for health, well over a decade and a half ago, on a voluntary basis. With an expectation that uptake by industry would have reached about 70% by this year. It’s about half of that. So the assistant minister for health, working with her colleagues, has indicated that front of pack labelling that tells parents exactly what is in the food they’re putting in the trolley will be made mandatory.

Albanese says no influence from industry over gambling policy

The independent MP Andrew Wilkie has alleged that “individuals in the Federal Government” had been “improperly influenced by individuals in the private sector” in formulating the gambling legislation, and written to the National Anti-Corruption Commission with his claims.

He asks the prime minister: “Do you agree this constitutes corruption? Do you understand how the donations have compromised your government and its judgment?”

The leader of the House, Tony Burke, takes issue with the question and the Speaker, Milton Dick, rules that he’ll rule out the reflection at the end.

Anthony Albanese says there’s no suggestion of wrongdoing in Wilkie’s letter to the Nacc, and that he doesn’t believe there has been any undue influence on his policy.

He then punts some of the responsibility of dealing with gambling harm over to the states.

I don’t suggest members on any side of this debate have been influenced. Other than by how do we deal with an issue that is complex, it isn’t simple, overwhelmingly, as the member full well knows, and was experienced in the last parliament. The major issue of addiction and problem gambling is poker machines, which are not dealt with by this jurisdiction but are dealt with by state and territory governments.

On political donations, he says they’re a matter for the party organisation and won’t say any more on that.

While he goes over his three-minute time limit, Dan Tehan starts coughing loudly.

australia.title: Japanese ambassador to Australia downplays Albanese melon gaffe as Taylor claims PM has ‘stuffed up’
australia.snippet: Coalition demands police investigate apparent leaking of diplomatic cable to newspaper but Labor calls it a ‘silly political stunt’ Follo...
australia.content:
The Japanese ambassador has downplayed Anthony Albanese’s comments about a gift of melons from Sanae Takaichi, saying Tokyo had been reassured by the Australian government that the prime minister “did not make the comments in the way that has been reported”.

While the Coalition continued to raise outrage over Albanese’s comments to the Bush Deep podcast, including seeking to have federal police investigate the alleged leaking of a diplomatic cable to a newspaper, the Japanese government appeared to be uninterested in making a diplomatic incident out of the much-maligned comments.

“We have been informed by the Australian side that Prime Minister Albanese did not make the comments in the way that has been reported,” said Kazuhiro Suzuki, the Japanese ambassador to Australia, in a statement on Wednesday afternoon.

The podcast comments – being referred to as “melon-gate” in Parliament House – dominated federal politics for another day on Wednesday, with Albanese maintaining he had nothing to apologise for.

“We take our relationships seriously, including our regular engagement with Japan. And that is why we will always put the national interest first and we continue to do so,” Albanese told parliament.

“The prime minister of Japan is a good friend of Australia … She was a welcome guest here.”

During an interview on the comedy podcast Bush Deep in early July, Albanese spoke about Japan’s leader, Takaichi, giving him a gift of Japanese melons. Discussing the present, he appeared to make hand gestures in front of his chest, saying “she brought two, as you do”. Host Nikki Osborne joked: “She came in looking like Pamela Anderson.”

The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, again demanded the prime minister apologise, claiming he had “stuffed up”. The senior shadow ministers Ted O’Brien and James Paterson demanded the Australian federal police investigate the apparent leaking of a diplomatic cable to The Australian newspaper, suggesting officers check whether the prime minister’s office was involved.

The AFP was contacted for comment and has not confirmed if it will investigate the matter.

The diplomatic cable was reportedly sent in July, days after the podcast, with Japan’s government saying there had been “sensationalised reporting in the Australian media” and that Tokyo believed there was no “ill intention” in Albanese’s actions.

After that development, the Coalition shifted to questioning how the document became public, claiming its publication was an “apparent unlawful disclosure of confidential correspondence from the government of Japan”.

“This is a serious matter. It is important that our closest allies have confidence of when they share confidential correspondence with us that it will not find its way in the media,” Paterson said.

But asked about whether the cable proved Japan was not worried about Albanese’s actions, O’Brien responded: “I won’t be commenting on how Tokyo interprets this entire saga.”

Labor ministers again lined up to defend Albanese on Wednesday. The housing minister, Clare O’Neil, called the Coalition’s AFP referral a “silly political stunt”, claiming the opposition had “completely lost the plot”. The education minister, Jason Clare, called it “rubbish”.

“The fact that the Liberal party seem to be distracted by this, I think, shows they’re not fit to govern here,” he said.

Albanese also shrugged off the Coalition concerns, saying the AFP was independent and would investigate whatever it deemed appropriate.

Japan’s government refrained from public comments on the issue until Wednesday, when its current ambassador to Australia released a statement not raising any further issue with Albanese’s conduct.

Suzuki noted Takaichi had visited Australia in May – shortly before the interview in question – and had been hosted for dinner by Albanese “in a very relaxed atmosphere, and we believe it helped build a personal trust relationship between the two leaders”.

The melon comments resurfaced as a political issue after The Australian ran a comment piece on Monday from the former Japanese ambassador Shingo Yamagami, who left his post in 2023, who claimed Albanese had insulted Takaichi.

australia.title: Andrew Bragg stands by proposed migration limits – even as Liberal colleagues decline to back him in
australia.snippet: Angus Taylor and other Coalition members not supporting shadow housing minister’s target migration numbers, which would be the lowest fig...
australia.content:
The Liberal senator Andrew Bragg has stood by his proposal to lower net migration to 180,000 a year in a wide-ranging speech where he lamented not stopping the Morrison government’s “madness” – even as colleagues side-stepped supporting the target figure publicly.

The opposition frontbencher said a housing “shortfall” – comparing the number of dwellings against population size – could be rectified if the net overseas migration (Nom) target was set at 180,000 or under over four years.

The reduction would bring the country to its lowest Nom figure since the mid-2000s.

“A Nom reduction on this scale is manageable and in line with reductions we’ve seen in the past – for example, in 2009-10 when Nom declined from 300,000 to 175,000 in 18 months,” Bragg said in his address at the National Press Club on Wednesday.

“This reduction can be achieved by getting the requisite skill changes that industry needs by having modest reductions in international students, working holidaymakers, and some unskilled workers.

“Lifting migration standards and analysing them carefully each year is crucial to ensure integrity and public trust in our migration settings.”

The Nom figure surged drastically after the pandemic, during which it fell below zero, but has began to return to more typical levels in recent quarters.

Under the Albanese government’s settings, the Nom is forecast to drop to 295,000 people last financial year; to 245,000 in 2026-27; and 225,000 in 2027-28.

Bragg admitted the opposition hadn’t yet finalised its “complete policy” on migration but he felt it was “important to move the debate” on to more details.

“We’re trying to get to a more sophisticated understanding of this nexus between housing and migration,” the shadow housing minister said.

“I think that the ministers of the day or the people who want to be ministers need to engage in the detail and say, ‘this is what I think we need to try and achieve. This is the range that we’re shooting for’.”

The Coalition has so far been reluctant to provide an exact figure for its Nom target, but the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, has indicated it will be “well below 200,000”.

“We will have an exact number when we go into the next election campaign, because we’ll know how many houses are built,” Taylor told 2GB radio.

The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, also declined to back his colleague’s proposed target, saying “I don’t think you should bank that at all” when asked if it was finalised policy.

“We haven’t made an announcement about where we’re going to be going into the next election, but our focus is actually about what we need to do to invest in the long-term growth and success of our country,” he told News24.

The shadow education minister, Julian Leeser, told an education conference the Nom must be lowered and that “international education must be part of the balance”.

The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, ruled out any cuts to visas that might affect the number of migrant workers employed by farmers, or in rural and regional areas.

Meanwhile, One Nation has said it will cap visas to 130,000 a year but has not provided any detail or clarity on which areas would be targeted.

The housing minister, Clare O’Neil, agreed migration is “a piece of the puzzle” when it comes to housing, but said politicians shouldn’t be allowed to “overstate the impact”.

Bragg’s speech outlined a number of policy ideas, including stripping the National Construction Code from more than one thousand pages down to 80 and a flatter tax structure for higher-earning individuals.

Bragg also acknowledged the role he played in former Coalition governments, including the Morrison government’s inability to get the federal budget into a promised surplus.

“As someone who was a backbencher in the Morrison government, I am sorry I didn’t do more to stop the madness,” he said.

“I believe the new liberalism Australia needs isn’t socialism and it isn’t conservatism seeking to turn back the clock.

“The madness started when Canberra gave up on the budget … whenever a politician announces more spending, they are stealing from tomorrow because there is no intention to balance the books.”

world.title: Spain to introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy
world.snippet: Move comes in response to Rome imposing similar measures after mass migration rush to Ceuta Spain has announced it will introduce tempora...
world.content:
Spain has announced it will introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy in response to Rome imposing similar measures after a mass rush of people from Morocco into Ceuta.

The checks, which come “amid the persistent irregular migration pressure” facing Italy, will start at midnight on Saturday and last until 7 September, Spain’s interior ministry said in a statement.

Hours earlier, Spain threatened Italy with countermeasures if it did not swiftly lift its own border checks, drawing a rebuff from Rome.

The rare spat between the EU and Nato allies came after tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco to Spain’s north African territory on 30-31 July in an unprecedented, deadly rush.

The scenes infuriated EU members that back a hard line on irregular immigration, including Italy, which imposed border checks on people arriving from Spain for one month.

The Spanish government criticised the measure on Friday as “unfair, contrary to the EU’s interests and discriminatory for the Spanish population”.

Foreign minister José Manuel Albares described it as “a torpedo fired at the hull of European unity”.

“We urge the government of Italy to rectify, put an end to the checks and treat Spaniards like other European citizens,” he added.

He threatened “proportional measures” in response by Sunday if Italy failed to comply.

Within hours, the government of Italy’s far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said it “had no intention of revising the decision” before 15 August, when it said Spanish authorities “expected a new wave of migration” to hit Ceuta.

Meloni’s office said in a statement: “Italy does not accept ultimatums or impositions from abroad regarding national security and border control.

“Only when there is certainty that there are no security or terrorism risks to Italy, that no new wave is occurring, and that no irregular migrants are heading toward European territory, will the decision be reconsidered.”

Spain’s interior ministry announced the reciprocal measures within hours.

Spanish police have been monitoring online rumours and social media about possible fresh arrivals in Ceuta in mid-August, according to local media. But authorities have not expressly said they expect a repeat of last week’s rush.

Border authorities would in the meantime “do their utmost to ensure maximum ease of movement for Spanish and European citizens” who are not affected by border checks, the Italian statement added.

Italy, which does not share a land border with Spain, introduced border controls at maritime and air entry points for third-country nationals arriving from Spain.

The move, announced on 31 July, was an “extraordinary measure” intended to “safeguard national security and prevent possible repercussions for our nation”, Meloni said at the time.

She was among several EU leaders who called for Spain to be suspended from the visa-free Schengen travel zone after the Ceuta incident, despite such a move being legally impossible.

Italy’s coalition government has sought to stop the tens of thousands of people who land in small boats on the country’s shores each year.

The Spanish government warned against “creating rifts and sterile conflicts driven by internal electoral motives” and said “we trust that pro-European sentiment, common sense and good faith prevail”.

Of the 72,000 people who entered Ceuta, 70,000 have returned to Morocco, according to official Spanish figures.

Spanish authorities said 80 people died in the crossings.

Moroccan rights groups, however, estimate the figure to be higher. The Moroccan Association for Human Rights and the European Coordination for Human Rights in Morocco on Friday said at least 141 deaths were recorded and that the toll was likely to rise.

Morocco’s interior ministry has said 11 people died on its side of the border, all but one by drowning.

Those who remain in Ceuta – including hundreds of unaccompanied children – face dire living conditions with little access to food, water and shelter.

world.title: Judge approves Trump effort to end South Sudan TPS protections
world.snippet: Decision follows supreme court ruling that allowed US government to strip protections for Haitians and Syrians Temporary protected status...
world.content:
Temporary protected status (TPS) for hundreds of South Sudanese nationals in the United States is set to end after a federal judge ruled that the Trump administration can move forward with stripping their protections.

On Friday, US district judge Patti Saris of the district of Massachusetts rejected an attempt by immigrant rights organizations including the New York-based African Communities Together to keep TPS for South Sudanese nationals living in the US.

Saris’s decision follows a 6-3 supreme court ruling in June allowing the Trump administration to strip hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians of TPS, which granted them permission to work and live legally in the US.

The supreme court’s conservative majority overturned lower court rulings in New York and Washington DC, which had blocked the administration from ending TPS for more than 350,000 Haitians and about 6,100 Syrians.

A TPS designation allows eligible people from certain countries facing crises including civil war and environmental disasters to remain in the US temporarily, protects them from deportation and allows them to work legally.

In her 15-page ruling, Saris wrote that “as a logical matter, plaintiffs’ arguments rest upon a self-contradictory, self-defeating foundation”.

According to Saris, the plaintiffs’ argument undermined itself, because if the homeland security department (DHS) lacked the authority to terminate South Sudan’s TPS designation, it also would have lacked the authority to issue the designation initially.

“South Sudan’s original TPS designation would thus be invalid by the same token as its termination,” Saris wrote.

In response to the ruling, James Percival, a DHS general counsel said on X: “Every other TPS judge must do the same! Every day these ‘administrative stays’ are in effect is a day the American people are denied what they voted for.”

The Guardian has contacted African Communities Together for comment.

Meanwhile, in a statement on Friday, the immigrant advocacy organization Global Refuge condemned the ruling. The CEO, Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, said: “The reality of the situation is that South Sudan is on the brink of a return to an all-out-civil war. Roughly two-thirds of the population, some 10 million people, now depend on humanitarian aid to survive.

“With only several hundred South Sudanese holding TPS in the US right now, this isn’t a policy forced by scale or strain on our system. To the contrary, this is the administration’s deliberate choice to send a small group of vulnerable individuals and families back into a country where civilians are bearing the brunt of intensifying violence and displacement,” Vignarajah added.

The Trump administration’s effort to strip TPS protections from hundreds of thousands of immigrants comes despite the US government’s own highest-level travel warnings for Americans to several countries affected, including South Sudan, Haiti and Syria.

In the case of South Sudan, the country has been ravaged by years of civil war and political instability that have displaced millions. Since gaining independence in 2011, more than 400,000 people have been killed in conflict, with fighting and ethnic violence continuing to claim civilian lives.

The DHS moved in November to terminate TPS for South Sudan, saying the country ‌no longer met the conditions for the designation, which was first issued in 2011. The department’s action would have led to the end of protections for more than 232 South Sudanese and at least 73 South Sudanese with pending applications. An earlier order by Saris had blocked that from happening.

After the supreme court’s ruling, lawyers for a group of South Sudanese nationals and the non-profit African Communities Together urged Saris to once again block the ‌end of TPS on new grounds that the justices had not addressed.

That included an argument that the DHS lacked authority to terminate TPS because the statute that created the TPS program in 1990 referred ​only to the attorney general as the official who had authority to extend and terminate the deportation protections.

The DHS was established later, in 2002, after the September 11 attacks.

Most of the justice department’s immigration-related functions were transferred to it at that time. Saris, who was appointed by Bill Clinton, concluded Congress had likewise transferred authority over TPS to the DHS.

Since 2001, TPS holders have paid $7.8bn annually in taxes and contributed $262bn to the US economy, according to the advocacy organization Fwd.us. Many TPS holders are employed in critical industries already facing worker shortages across the country, including construction, hospitality and healthcare.

Losing TPS can leave immigrants without legal status vulnerable to arrest, detention and deportation, even with pending asylum or green card applications.

Some may face immigration court proceedings with limited options to stay in the US. People ordered removed could be deported and barred from returning for years.

Reuters contributed reporting

world.title: Ebola virus behind massive outbreak in DRC could be mutating, officials say
world.snippet: Cases have passed 4,000 and health watchdog plans to go door to door to find patients in major response escalation The virus causing a ma...
world.content:
The virus causing a massive outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo could be mutating, health officials fear, as confirmed cases pass 4,000.

Africa’s public health watchdog said the time for incremental action was over as they announced plans to scale up every aspect of the response and go “door to door” looking for patients.

The Ebola outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, was first reported on 15 May, although there are suspicions the disease could have been spreading since January.

There have been 3,973 cases and 1,801 deaths recorded as of 4 August, according to the DRC’s national public health institute. Speaking on Thursday, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), told a press briefing cases had topped 4,000.

The outbreak is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. There are eight times more cases, and six times more deaths than were recorded 11 weeks into the West Africa Ebola outbreak in 2014-18, which infected more than 28,000 people and killed at least 11,000.

Kaseya said he had spoken to the director general of the World Health Organization, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, and they planned studies “to check if there is no additional issue, or maybe if the virus is not mutating. Because the level of severity of this Bundibugyo outbreak is unprecedented.”

More than two-thirds of Ebola deaths are happening in the community rather than in treatment centres. In a treatment centre run by MSF in Bunia, the capital of Ituri province, 90% of admitted patients do not appear on authorities’ lists of contacts of known cases. Both factors indicate high levels of untracked transmission.

Kaseya said contact tracing in the DRC was insufficient, with only 10 contacts identified for every Ebola patient, when about 40 would be the expected number.

Ebola is a viral haemorrhagic fever that can cause vomiting, diarrhoea, organ damage and internal bleeding. The outbreak is centred on the conflict-affected mining province of Ituri, but has spread to Nord-Kivu, Sud-Kivu, Haut-Uele and Tshopo. There were 20 cases recorded in neighbouring Uganda before it brought its outbreak under control.

Dr Wessam Mankoula, acting head of emergency preparedness and response at Africa CDC, said response teams planned a shift “from contact tracing to active case search”, which would mean community health workers “moving from door to door” asking households if they had anyone sick with Ebola symptoms.

He added: “I think the time for incremental action is over and we’re starting now the phase for scaling up.”

Kaseya promised a “village-centered response” that would involve communities, more use of digital tools and greater action in the camps for people who have been internally displaced by conflict in affected provinces.

Officials also said they planned to begin using antiviral remdesivir on a compassionate use basis to treat patients. They will also start testing whether Ervebo, a vaccine licensed for use against a different strain of Ebola, should be offered in the affected province, after receiving data suggesting that Bundibugyo caused less serious disease and “zero death” among people who had received that jab.

“Seeing the expansion of this outbreak, only the public health measure will not be enough to quickly control or stop this outbreak,” said Dr Placide Mbala Kingebeni, Africa CDC director of research, clinical trials and innovation.

DRC authorities said they were investigating a suspected Ebola death on a boat heading to the capital, Kinshasa, from the north-east of the country, and that the other passengers on board would be quarantined and tested.

Unicef warned that essential healthcare was being disrupted by the outbreak as fear of infection and service disruptions kept families away from clinics. In the outbreak’s centre, the mining town of Mongbwalu, the proportion of children receiving their first measles dose has fallen 69%.

world.title: US to shut five consulates as critics fear China could fill diplomatic vacuum
world.snippet: State department informs Congress of planned closures in Canada, Grenada, Japan, Indonesia and Cameroon The US state department is to shu...
world.content:
The US state department is to shut five foreign consulates and missions across Asia, Africa, North America and the Caribbean, drawing criticism that it is leaving a diplomatic vacuum at risk of being filled by China.

The US Congress has been served notice of the impending closures, which are being justified on cost grounds and follow a reassessment of the US’s bilateral relationships with a range of countries since Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

According to a notice served to several congressional committees, missions will close in St George’s, Grenada; Nagoya, Japan; Medan, Indonesia; Douala, Cameroon; and Winnipeg, Canada.

The closures will continue a process of cutbacks in US state department operations overseen by Marco Rubio, the secretary of state. Last year, the department fired more than 1,300 employees, including 246 foreign services officers and 1,107 civil servants.

More than half of the US’s 195 ambassadorial posts around the world remain unfilled, including in keys locations such as Germany, Cuba, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, according to the American Foreign Service Association.

Democrats have criticized the latest planned closures, saying it risked leaving the field free for China.

“China has a diplomatic presence in three of the five locations where the state department is closing shop and Beijing is going to exploit that new vacuum to undercut American interests,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee.

“The yearly operating costs of these diplomatic facilities represent a tiny fraction of the state department’s yearly budget,” Shaheen added. “Is that worth pulling back from these places where China is present?”

The decision to close the consulate in Winnipeg has come in for criticism in Canada, on which Trump recently announced the imposition of 50% tariffs on a range of goods.

Opened in 2001, the Winnipeg consulate has served to facilitate trade and investment issues mainly relating to the province of Manitoba, of which Winnipeg is the capital.

Brad Kirbyson, a former political specialist who worked at the consulate for 20 years, told the Canadian broadcaster CBC the closure could harm US interests.

“I’m sure it’ll save them a few dollars, but I think the net effect is to lose touch with a broad swath of Canada by not having a presence there,” he said. “The United States found that it was a very long way between the US consulate in Calgary and the [one] in Toronto.

“It makes a lot of sense to have a consulate in the middle of the country that can cover issues in this part of the world.”

A spokesperson for the Canadian embassy in Washington said: “Canada and the US have a long history of collaboration on areas of shared interest, including through our foreign offices in both countries.”

China does not have a diplomatic mission in Winnipeg, but it has a presence in St George’s, Nagoya and Medan. The US mission in St George’s, the capital of the Caribbean island of Grenada, has full embassy status, while the Douala facility is defined as an “embassy branch office”.

A state department spokesperson said: “The department is committed to following congressional notification procedures including post closures. We have nothing further to report at this time.

“We are focused on ensuring our diplomatic footprint is efficient, effective and delivers results for the American people.”

In a later statement, issued after this story was first published, a department spokesperson countered the assertion that the closures would benefit China.

“Claims that China is filling a diplomatic vacuum is [sic] inherently false and we recommend that individuals who subscribe to this propaganda take a look at the so-called help China had in the recent earthquakes in Venezuela or to address the Ebola outbreak,” the spokesperson said.

The White House’s office of management and budget has argued for a much more extensive closure program of up to 30 foreign missions.

Democrats, supported by national security and foreign policy specialists, have countered that such moves will dangerously reduce the US’s diplomatic footprint and global influence, especially when combined with last year’s dismantling of USAID, the main overseas development body, which was drastically reduced in size before being bundled into the state department.

world.title: Top Ugandan footballer killed by robbers armed with paving stones
world.snippet: David Owori, who played for the national team, died in hospital after he tried to stop robbers taking his phone The Ugandan football comm...
world.content:
The Ugandan football community is in mourning after the death of a player who was fatally injured during a robbery in the capital, Kampala, on Tuesday night.

David Owori, who captained Sports Club Villa, a Uganda Premier League club, and represented the national team, was attacked after resisting an attempt to steal his mobile phone and other belongings near his home in Makindye division.

Racheal Kawala, a spokesperson for the Kampala Metropolitan police, said he was found unconscious by ​passersby, who took him to a nearby hospital. He was ​transferred to another hospital, where he was pronounced dead on Wednesday.

Witnesses said attackers hit the footballer with paving stones before robbing him and fleeing, leaving him unconscious, the BBC reported.

Owori, 27, was a right-back and midfielder for SC Villa. He helped the team win a record 17th Uganda Premier League title in 2024.

He started his senior career in 2016 at the Uganda Premier League side Vipers Sports Club and had stints in Europe with Vélez CF in Spain and Utsiktens BK in Sweden.

He played for the national team in the qualifiers for the 2021 Africa Cup of Nations.

SC Villa said: “It is with profound sorrow that we announce the untimely passing of our captain, Owori, who had been receiving treatment at Case Clinic following an attack by suspected thugs. Our deepest condolences and prayers are with his family.”

The Federation ​of Uganda Football Associations said: “David was not just a footballer. He was ​both a leader and an inspiration to a generation. As ​Captain of SC Villa, he led with courage, humility and passion. In the Uganda Cranes jersey, he carried the hopes of a nation.”

It added: “We have lost a son, a leader and a star. His light on and off the pitch will never be forgotten.”

The Ugandan parliament observed a minute of silence in Owori’s honour on Wednesday.

In June Sydney Gongodyo, a Ugandan rugby international, ​died after a mob attacked him in Kampala, mistaking him for a thief, police said.

Uganda’s National Council of Sports said: “Sadly, ​Ugandan sport has been hit with many such ​tragedies lately, and we hope for justice and a lasting solution.”
